claims.evidence: This describes neutralization data for a chimeric antibody and draws a conclusion about the importance of heavy chain maturation.

claims.claim: Affinity maturation of the heavy chain is critical for imparting both binding and neutralization.
claims.source: The inferred naive heavy chain paired with the mature light chain (0VHmatVL) did not result in any detectable neutralization of the virus panel (Figure 2D), suggesting that affinity maturation of the heavy chain is critical for imparting both binding and neutralization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neutralization data for various antibody chain pairings.

claims.claim: When Int5VL was paired with the mature heavy chain (matVH Int5VL), there was an average fourfold increase in neutralization potency for all viruses tested compared to matVH0VL.
claims.source: When Int5VL was paired with the mature heavy chain (matVH Int5VL), there was an average fourfold increase in neutralization potency for all viruses tested compared to matVH0VL (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the contribution of light chain maturation to neutralization potency.

claims.claim: A 4.15 Å cryo-EM structure of QA013.2 Fab bound to BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer was obtained.
claims.source: To better identify which residues contribute to QA013.2's ability to bind and neutralize Env, we performed single particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) on the QA013.2 Fab and BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer complex (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This describes the structural study performed, with the resolution stated in the abstract and methods.

claims.claim: The known structure of BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (PDB ID: 5aco) was fit into the resulting 4.15 Å resolution EM density map along with a homology model for the variable domain of QA013.2 Fab.
claims.source: The known structure of BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (PDB ID: 5aco) was fit into the resulting 4.15 Å resolution EM density map along with a homology model for the variable domain of QA013.2 Fab (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This describes the structural modeling approach used.

claims.claim: The complex structure of QA013.2 Fab bound to BG505.SOSIP.664 delineated antigen contacts characteristic of other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs, including conserved glycans as well as the linear GDIR motif.
claims.source: The complex structure of QA013.2 Fab bound to BG505.SOSIP.664 delineated antigen contacts characteristic of other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs, including conserved glycans as well as the linear GDIR motif (Barnes et al., 2018; Mouquet et al., 2012; Pejchal et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes the structural features observed and compares them to other known antibodies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: QA013.2 interacts not only with the N332 glycan as previously reported, but also with the glycan at site N301, and the linear GDIR motif at the base of the V3 loop.
claims.source: From the cryo-EM structure, it is apparent that QA013.2 interacts not only with the N332 glycan as previously reported (Williams et al., 2018), but also with the glycan at site N301, and the linear GDIR motif at the base of the V3 loop (Figure 3C–E).
claims.evidence: This describes the epitope contacts observed in the structure, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Key regions of the antibody paratope include the CDRH1 and CDRH2 which are nearest the N301 glycan, as well as CDRH3 and CDRL3, which are in close proximity to the N332 glycan.
claims.source: Key regions of the antibody paratope include the CDRH1 and CDRH2 which are nearest the N301 glycan, as well as CDRH3 and CDRL3, which are in close proximity to the N332 glycan.
claims.evidence: This describes the structural organization of the antibody-antigen interface.

claims.claim: The CDR loops of the heavy chain contain many polar and charged residues, which likely facilitate hydrogen bonding interaction with the Env glycans and the charged residues in the GDIR motif.
claims.source: We observe that the CDR loops of the heavy chain contain many polar and charged residues, which likely facilitate hydrogen bonding interaction with the Env glycans and the charged residues in the GDIR motif (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the chemical properties of the paratope and infers their functional role.

claims.claim: The CDRH3 loop is distinctively long (21 residues) and appears to tilt away from the rest of the heavy chain toward the light chain, generating a cleft between CDRH2 and CDRH3.
claims.source: The CDRH3 loop is distinctively long (21 residues) and appears to tilt away from the rest of the heavy chain toward the light chain, generating a cleft between CDRH2 and CDRH3 and exposing an extended interface that has been observed for other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs including 10–1074 and PGT121 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Mouquet et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This describes a structural feature of the antibody and compares it to other known antibodies, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Seven key residues in the Fab CDRH3 loop (L103 – I109) lie adjacent to the conserved GDIR motif.
claims.source: Seven key residues in the Fab CDRH3 loop (L103 – I109) lie adjacent to the conserved GDIR motif.
claims.evidence: This describes specific residues in the structure that are near the GDIR motif.

claims.claim: Based on sequencing data of the sampled repertoire, these amino acids (excluding Y105 and D107) were likely introduced during affinity maturation of the heavy chain between 765 dpii and 2282 dpii because they were not detected by NGS through 765 dpii.
claims.source: Based on our sequencing data of the sampled repertoire of this subject, these amino acids (excluding Y105 and D107) were likely introduced during affinity maturation of the heavy chain between 765 dpii and 2282 dpii because they were not detected by NGS through 765 dpii (Figure 1C), suggesting a potential role for these residues in facilitating antibody breadth and/or potency.
claims.evidence: This infers the timing of when specific mutations arose based on sequencing data.

claims.claim: Mutations in individual CDRs, including adjacent FWR mutations, were not sufficient to achieve potent neutralization comparable to the mature antibody when paired with the mature light chain.
claims.source: Mutations in individual CDRs, including adjacent FWR mutations, were not sufficient to achieve potent neutralization comparable to the mature antibody when paired with the mature light chain.
claims.evidence: This describes the results of chimeric antibody experiments testing individual CDR contributions.

claims.claim: Weak autologous neutralization was observed when mutations surrounding FWRH3-CDRH3 were added to Int6VH.
claims.source: We did observe weak autologous neutralization when mutations surrounding FWRH3-CDRH3 were added to Int6VH.
claims.evidence: This describes the results of a specific chimeric antibody experiment.

claims.claim: Mutations spanning both FWRH1-CDRH1 and FWRH3-CDRH3 of the mature VH together were required to obtain heterologous neutralization.
claims.source: Mutations spanning both FWRH1-CDRH1 and FWRH3-CDRH3 of the mature VH together were required to obtain heterologous neutralization, consistent with the cryo-EM map of key antigen contacts (Figures 3 and 4A).
claims.evidence: This describes the results of chimeric antibody experiments and relates them to structural data.

claims.claim: The determinants of autologous and heterologous neutralization in this antibody lineage were different, in which autologous virus neutralization required less SHM and was facilitated by residues spanning CDRH2-FWRH3-CDRH3.
claims.source: Interestingly, the determinants of autologous and heterologous neutralization in this antibody lineage were different, in which autologous virus neutralization required less SHM and was facilitated by residues spanning CDRH2-FWRH3-CDRH3 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This describes a key finding about the different requirements for autologous versus heterologous neutralization.

claims.claim: Reversion of all framework mutations in the mature VH back to the inferred naive BCR residues (∆FWR) resulted in no detectable binding or neutralization activity.
claims.source: To determine the importance of the framework residues and examine loss of function, we reverted all framework mutations in the mature VH back to the inferred naive BCR residues (∆FWR). This reversion resulted in no detectable binding or neutralization activity, demonstrating that residues in the heavy chain FWRs are essential for QA013.2 binding and neutralization, as has been noted for other HIV bnAbs (Figure 4A,B; Klein et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This describes the results of a reversion experiment and compares to other antibodies, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Residues in the heavy chain FWRs are essential for QA013.2 binding and neutralization.
claims.source: To determine the importance of the framework residues and examine loss of function, we reverted all framework mutations in the mature VH back to the inferred naive BCR residues (∆FWR). This reversion resulted in no detectable binding or neutralization activity, demonstrating that residues in the heavy chain FWRs are essential for QA013.2 binding and neutralization, as has been noted for other HIV bnAbs (Figure 4A,B; Klein et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reversion experiment.

claims.claim: Reversion of FWRH1 mutations resulted in a 733-fold increase in IC50 for neutralization of clade C virus QC406.F3.
claims.source: We also observed a dramatic reduction in heterologous virus neutralization for these same VH chimeric antibodies (∆FWRH1 or ∆CDRH1). Specifically, we observed 733-fold and 250-fold increases in the IC50 for ∆FWRH1 and ∆CDRH1 chimeric antibodies respectively, corresponding to decreased neutralization of clade C virus QC406.F3 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRH1 mutations on heterologous neutralization.

claims.claim: Reversion of FWRH1-CDRH1 mutations resulted in a 250-fold increase in IC50 for neutralization of clade C virus QC406.F3.
claims.source: We also observed a dramatic reduction in heterologous virus neutralization for these same VH chimeric antibodies (∆FWRH1 or ∆CDRH1). Specifically, we observed 733-fold and 250-fold increases in the IC50 for ∆FWRH1 and ∆CDRH1 chimeric antibodies respectively, corresponding to decreased neutralization of clade C virus QC406.F3 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRH1-CDRH1 mutations on heterologous neutralization.

claims.claim: Reversion of the six residues spanning FWRH1-CDRH1 led to weakened binding to heterologous BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (KD = 40.6 nM) relative to the mature bnAb.
claims.source: Reversion of the six residues spanning FWRH1-CDRH1 also led to weakened binding to heterologous BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (KD = 40.6 nM) relative to the mature bnAb (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRH1-CDRH1 mutations on binding affinity.

claims.claim: When the CDRH3 was reverted back to naïve (∆CDR3VH), binding and neutralization of both autologous and heterologous virus was maintained, but there was an impact on potency across all viruses tested.
claims.source: When the CDRH3 was reverted back to naïve (∆CDR3VH), binding and neutralization of both autologous and heterologous virus was maintained, but there was an impact on potency across all viruses tested; although this antibody could still neutralize a heterologous clade C variant, it did not neutralize SF162 at the highest antibody concentration tested (Figures 3 and 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This describes the effect of reverting CDRH3 mutations on neutralization.

claims.claim: The CDRH3 does contribute to the overall breadth and potency of QA013.2, while mutations in FWRH1-CDRH1 are critical for achieving complete cross-clade Tier two neutralization breadth.
claims.source: These data suggest that the CDRH3 does contribute to the overall breadth and potency of QA013.2, while mutations in FWRH1-CDRH1 are critical for achieving complete cross-clade Tier two neutralization breadth.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimeric antibody experiments.

claims.claim: Four of the six residues spanning FWRH1-CDRH1 individually contributed to the mature bnAb's ability to neutralize autologous and heterologous virus.
claims.source: We found that four of the six residues spanning FWRH1-CDRH1 individually contributed to the mature bnAb's ability to neutralize autologous and heterologous virus.
claims.evidence: This describes the results of point mutation experiments.

claims.claim: Residues E26, G28, and I24 were most critical, with average increase in IC50 of 191-, 27-, and 25-fold, respectively, across all pseudoviruses tested when these residues were reverted to naïve.
claims.source: Residues E26, G28, and I24 were most critical, with average increase in IC50 of 191-, 27-, and 25-fold, respectively, across all pseudoviruses tested when these residues were reverted to naïve (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the contribution of specific residues to neutralization potency.

claims.claim: Reversion of individual CDRH3 residues did not abolish neutralization.
claims.source: While reversion of individual CDRH3 residues did not abolish neutralization, which correlates with the chimeric antibody results (Figure 4), one residue in particular (D106) demonstrated a much higher IC50 value when mutated back to naive.

claims.claim: D106 is adjacent to the GDIR motif in the structure.
claims.source: D106 is adjacent to the GDIR motif in the structure.
claims.evidence: This describes the structural location of residue D106.

claims.claim: Reversion of D106 to naive did not inhibit clade A autologous virus neutralization, but did substantially impact heterologous neutralization, with an average 40-fold increase in IC50 across all tested pseudoviruses.
claims.source: Reversion of this residue to naive did not inhibit clade A autologous virus neutralization, but did substantially impact heterologous neutralization, with an average 40-fold increase in IC50 across all tested pseudoviruses (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This quantifies the effect of the D106V mutation on neutralization.

claims.claim: The D106V point mutant only resulted in a modest decrease in binding to heterologous BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer relative to the mature bnAb.

claims.evidence: This describes the binding effect of the D106V mutation.

claims.claim: While D106 is not critical for Env binding, this residue does contribute to heterologous neutralization, likely by interacting directly with the linear GDIR motif.
claims.source: These data suggest that while D106 is not critical for Env binding, this residue does contribute to heterologous neutralization, likely by interacting directly with the linear GDIR motif.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the D106V mutation data.

claims.claim: Although the antibody paratope of QA013.2 includes the CDRH3, where interaction with the N332 glycan and GDIR motif occurs, the QA013.2 paratope is also comprised of critical residues in FWRH1 and CDRH1.
claims.source: Taken together, it is clear that although the antibody paratope of QA013.2 includes the CDRH3, where interaction with the N332 glycan and GDIR motif occurs, the QA013.2 paratope is also comprised of critical residues in FWRH1 and CDRH1.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the mutagenesis experiments.

claims.claim: Reversion of residues spanning FWRL2-FWRL3 abrogated antibody binding to BG505.SOSIP.664 heterologous Env (KD = 1.3 µM) relative to the mature bnAb by more than 400-fold.
claims.source: Reversion of the residues spanning FWRL2-FWRL3 abrogated antibody binding to BG505.SOSIP.664 heterologous Env (KD = 1.3 µM) relative to the mature bnAb by more than 400-fold.
claims.evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRL2-FWRL3 mutations on binding affinity.

claims.claim: Reversion of residues present in FWRL2-FWRL3 resulted in an average 19-fold increase in IC50 (range 6–42 fold) across all pseudoviruses tested when compared to the mature bnAb IC50 values.
claims.source: Reversion of residues present in FWRL2-FWRL3 resulted in an average 19-fold increase in IC50 (range 6–42 fold) and reversion of residues in CDRL3 caused a 14-fold increase in average IC50 (range 1–41 fold) across all pseudoviruses tested when compared to the mature bnAb IC50 values (Figure 6A).

results.result: Subject QA013 was initially infected with HIV clade D in 1995, then superinfected with clade A between 264-385 dpii. Both viruses persisted for at least 6 years, and bnAb QA013.2 was isolated at 2282 dpii.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by citations to prior work (Chohan et al., 2005; Williams et al., 2018) and provide the clinical context for the study. The timeline and viral characteristics are clearly documented.

results.result: Deep sequencing of four longitudinal PBMC samples (pre-infection to 765 dpii) combined with computational lineage inference identified eight VH and six VL intermediate sequences between naive BCR and mature QA013.2, with several inferred sequences validated by ≥98% nucleotide identity to sampled sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C9 describe the sequencing and computational approach with appropriate methodological detail. The validation of inferred sequences against actual NGS data (C9) strengthens confidence in the computational predictions. Methods are cited (Dhar et al., 2020; Ralph and Matsen, 2016).

results.result: The QA013.2 heavy chain clonal family (42 members, top 10 largest) used VH3-7*01/VD1-1*01/VJ5*02 genes with 21-residue CDRH3 and accumulated 20% SHM (38 amino acid mutations). The light chain family (>1000 members, likely overclustered) used VL1-40*01/VJ2*01 genes and accumulated 12% SHM.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C16 provide detailed characterization of the antibody lineages. The authors acknowledge technical issues with light chain overclustering (C14), demonstrating appropriate critical assessment. The quantitative data on SHM and gene usage are clearly stated.

results.result: More than 70% of total SHM (84 of 117 nucleotide mutations) in QA013.2 was not detected in sequence data through 765 dpii, suggesting incomplete sampling or mutation accumulation between 765-2282 dpii.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 acknowledges a significant limitation in the lineage reconstruction - the majority of mutations occurred after the last sequencing timepoint. The authors appropriately present two possible explanations (incomplete sampling vs. late accumulation) without overinterpreting.

results.result: The inferred naive BCR showed weak but detectable binding to autologous clade A superinfecting virus gp120 and weaker binding to heterologous BG505 trimer, but no detectable binding to the clade D initial infecting virus, suggesting the lineage was initiated by the superinfecting virus.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 present BLI data showing differential binding of the naive BCR to different viral strains. The authors appropriately note that binding kinetics could not be reliably calculated (C18, C20), but the qualitative observation supports lineage initiation by the superinfecting virus. This is consistent with the neutralization profile.

results.result: The mature QA013.2 bnAb exhibited strong binding to both autologous SI gp120 (KD=94.9 nM) and heterologous BG505 trimer (KD=3.2 nM). Chimeric antibodies with mature VH paired with naive VL showed reduced binding (KD=89.6 nM to BG505), while naive VH with mature VL showed no binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 provide quantitative BLI data demonstrating the importance of heavy chain maturation for binding. The chimeric antibody experiments are well-designed to dissect chain-specific contributions. Quantitative KD values are provided where measurable.

results.result: The intermediate antibody Int6VHInt5VL (6% SHM, validated at 99-100% nucleotide identity to NGS sequences) bound heterologous BG505 trimer (KD=513 nM) but not autologous SI gp120, demonstrating that VH is important for HIV recognition and that early maturation enables measurable heterologous binding, though higher affinity required 30 additional non-synonymous mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 characterize an intermediate antibody with validated sequence identity to sampled repertoire. The binding data demonstrate progressive affinity maturation, with quantitative measurements supporting the conclusion that VH drives initial recognition. The requirement for additional mutations for high-affinity binding is clearly documented.

results.result: Neutralization assays showed that naive and intermediate antibodies could not neutralize virus despite some binding capacity. The mature VH paired with naive VL achieved autologous and heterologous neutralization, while naive VH with mature VL showed no neutralization, demonstrating that heavy chain maturation is critical for neutralization and that neutralization-mediating mutations were acquired between 765-2282 dpii. Light chain maturation (Int5VL) provided a 4-fold increase in potency.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 present systematic neutralization data from chimeric antibodies that clearly dissect the contributions of heavy and light chains. The experiments demonstrate that binding does not equal neutralization (C34) and that heavy chain maturation is necessary and sufficient for neutralization, while light chain maturation enhances potency. The inference about timing (C36) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: A 4.15 Å cryo-EM structure of QA013.2 Fab bound to BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer revealed characteristic V3/glycan-specific bnAb features including interactions with N301 and N332 glycans and the GDIR motif. The paratope includes CDRH1/CDRH2 (near N301), CDRH3/CDRL3 (near N332), with a distinctively long 21-residue CDRH3 that tilts toward the light chain, creating a cleft similar to other V3/glycan bnAbs.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 describe the cryo-EM structure with appropriate resolution (4.15 Å) and detail the epitope contacts. The structure is compared to other known V3/glycan bnAbs (10-1074, PGT121) with citations. The structural features are consistent with the functional data and provide molecular basis for understanding antibody-antigen interactions.

results.result: Seven key CDRH3 residues (L103-I109) lie adjacent to the GDIR motif, and most (excluding Y105 and D107) were likely introduced between 765-2282 dpii as they were not detected by NGS through 765 dpii.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 integrate structural and sequencing data to infer when specific mutations arose. The inference is reasonable given the absence of these residues in the sequenced repertoire, though the authors appropriately acknowledge this could reflect incomplete sampling (as noted in C17).

results.result: Chimeric antibody experiments showed that mutations in individual CDRs were insufficient for potent neutralization. Weak autologous neutralization required FWRH3-CDRH3 mutations, while heterologous neutralization required mutations spanning both FWRH1-CDRH1 and FWRH3-CDRH3. Autologous and heterologous neutralization had different determinants, with autologous requiring less SHM and being facilitated by CDRH2-FWRH3-CDRH3.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 present systematic mutagenesis data showing that multiple regions must work together for neutralization. The finding that autologous and heterologous neutralization have different requirements (C52) is well-supported by the chimeric antibody data and represents an important mechanistic insight.

results.result: Reversion of all framework mutations in mature VH to naive (ΔFWR) abolished all binding and neutralization activity, demonstrating that heavy chain framework residues are essential for QA013.2 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 demonstrate the critical importance of framework mutations through loss-of-function experiments. This finding is compared to other HIV bnAbs with appropriate citation (Klein et al., 2013), placing the result in broader context.

results.result: Reversion of FWRH1 or FWRH1-CDRH1 mutations resulted in 733-fold and 250-fold increases in IC50 for heterologous virus neutralization, respectively, and weakened binding to BG505 trimer (KD=40.6 nM for ΔCDRH1).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 provide quantitative data on the contribution of FWRH1-CDRH1 region to neutralization and binding. The large fold-changes in IC50 clearly demonstrate the importance of this region for heterologous neutralization breadth.

results.result: Reversion of CDRH3 to naive (ΔCDR3VH) maintained binding and neutralization of autologous and heterologous virus but reduced potency across all viruses tested. CDRH3 contributes to overall breadth and potency, while FWRH1-CDRH1 mutations are critical for complete cross-clade Tier 2 neutralization breadth.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 demonstrate that CDRH3, while important for potency, is not absolutely required for neutralization breadth. This contrasts with many other V3/glycan bnAbs and represents a key distinguishing feature of QA013.2. The data support the conclusion that FWRH1-CDRH1 is more critical for breadth.

results.result: Point mutation analysis showed that four of six FWRH1-CDRH1 residues individually contributed to neutralization, with E26, G28, and I24 being most critical (191-, 27-, and 25-fold average IC50 increases when reverted to naive).
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 provide fine-mapping of critical residues through systematic point mutagenesis. The quantitative fold-change data clearly identify E26 as the most critical residue, with G28 and I24 also important. This level of detail is valuable for understanding structure-function relationships.

results.result: Individual CDRH3 residue reversions did not abolish neutralization, but D106 (adjacent to GDIR motif) showed substantial impact on heterologous neutralization (40-fold average IC50 increase) without affecting autologous neutralization or causing major binding defects, suggesting D106 contributes to heterologous neutralization likely through direct interaction with the GDIR motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 identify D106 as a key CDRH3 residue for heterologous neutralization through systematic mutagenesis. The differential effect on autologous vs. heterologous neutralization and the modest binding effect support the interpretation that D106 specifically contributes to breadth through GDIR interaction.

results.result: The QA013.2 paratope comprises critical residues in FWRH1 and CDRH1 in addition to CDRH3 (which interacts with N332 glycan and GDIR motif).
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is a summary conclusion well-supported by the extensive mutagenesis data (C49-C68) and structural analysis (C40-C46). This represents a key finding distinguishing QA013.2 from other V3/glycan bnAbs.

results.result: Light chain mutagenesis showed that reversion of FWRL2-FWRL3 residues reduced binding >400-fold (KD=1.3 μM) and caused 19-fold average IC50 increase, while CDRL3 reversion caused 14-fold average IC50 increase. FWRL2-FWRL3 and CDRL3 contribute to binding affinity and neutralization potency, with FWRL2-FWRL3 having larger influence on binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 demonstrate light chain contributions to antibody function through systematic mutagenesis. The quantitative data clearly show that while the light chain is less critical than the heavy chain, FWRL2-FWRL3 residues make substantial contributions to binding affinity.

results.result: FWRL2-FWRL3 residues do not directly interact with N332 glycan but may influence CDRL3 conformation (which does interact with N332), and FWRL2 residues interact with FWRH4 of the heavy chain following CDRH3.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 provide structural interpretation of how FWRL2-FWRL3 contributes to function indirectly through conformational effects and inter-chain interactions. The structural observations (C76) support the functional data, though the conformational influence (C75) is appropriately stated as inference ('may influence').

results.result: Mutational antigenic profiling identified viral escape mutations in N301/N332 PNGS, GDIR motif, and V1 loop. Strongest enrichment was at D325, R327, and H330 (>32-fold IC50 change), though not all mutations at these sites caused escape. V1 escape occurred at D141 and R151 (~3-fold IC50 change).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 present comprehensive antigenic profiling data with validation by individual mutant testing. The identification of V1 escape mutations is novel for V3/glycan bnAbs. The authors appropriately note mutation-specific effects (C81-C82) and compare to other antibodies (10-1074) with citation.

results.result: While V1 loop does not appear in direct contact with QA013.2 Fab in the structure, the backbone Cα atoms of CDRH3 and V1 are within 8 Å, suggesting possible side-chain interactions affecting neutralization.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 provides structural context for the V1 escape mutations. The 8 Å distance measurement supports the possibility of side-chain interactions, though the authors appropriately state this as inference ('suggesting there could be'). This integrates structural and functional data.

results.result: The N332 glycan is essential for neutralization but not required for binding, as demonstrated by mature bnAb binding to clade D and BG505.W6.C1 gp120s lacking N332 PNGS, though this binding is too weak to confer neutralization.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 distinguish between binding and neutralization requirements for N332. The binding data for viruses lacking N332 (C86) support the conclusion, and the inference that weak binding is insufficient for neutralization (C87) is reasonable and confirms N332's importance.

results.result: Elimination of N301 glycan (N301K mutation) abolished all neutralization activity despite N332 presence, demonstrating that both N301 and N332 glycans are required in combination for bnAb neutralization.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 provide direct experimental evidence for N301 dependence through targeted mutagenesis. This complements the structural data (C43) showing N301 interaction and the antigenic profiling data (C78) showing N301 as an escape site. The conclusion is well-supported.

results.result: QA013.2 neutralized clade A but not clade D or D/A recombinant viruses. Clade A neutralization required N301, N332, and GDIR motif, and the mature bnAb only neutralizes viruses containing all three features.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 define the epitope requirements for neutralization through testing an expanded virus panel. The clade-specific neutralization pattern is consistent with the structural data and prior work (Williams et al., 2018). The requirement for all three features is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: All neutralized viruses (except MK184.W0.D1) contain a [negative charge/branched hydrophobic/positive charge] motif in the final 10 V1 residues. Four viruses with N301/N332/GDIR that were not neutralized either had subtype D V1/V2 or lacked this V1 motif. QA013.2 can only neutralize clades A, B, and C (not D), and V1 influences antibody function.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 identify a V1 sequence motif associated with neutralization sensitivity through systematic analysis of the virus panel. The pattern is well-documented with appropriate citation for virus characterization (Wu et al., 2006). This provides mechanistic insight into the V1 escape mutations and clade-specific neutralization.

results.result: BnAb QA013.2 bound both initial and superinfecting viral Env despite its naive progenitor only recognizing the superinfecting strain, suggesting both viruses influenced the lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 integrate binding data (C18-C22, C86) to conclude that both viruses influenced lineage development. The mature antibody's ability to bind the initial virus (which the naive BCR could not) suggests affinity maturation was influenced by both viral strains, though the inference is appropriately stated as 'suggesting'.

results.result: A 4.15 Å cryo-EM structure showed QA013.2 recognition of V3 signatures (N301/N332 and GDIR).
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is directly supported by the structural data (C40-C43). The resolution is appropriate for identifying these interactions, and the structure is consistent with functional data.

results.result: QA013.2 relies less on CDRH3 and more on framework and CDRH1 for affinity and breadth compared to other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is well-supported by the extensive mutagenesis data (C49-C69) showing that CDRH3 reversion maintains neutralization while FWRH1-CDRH1 reversion abolishes breadth. This represents a key distinguishing feature of QA013.2 compared to other V3/glycan bnAbs.

results.result: Viral escape was achieved by changes in the structurally-defined epitope and by mutations in V1.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is supported by the antigenic profiling data (C77-C83) showing escape mutations in both the core epitope (N301, N332, GDIR) and the V1 loop. The V1 escape is novel for V3/glycan bnAbs.

results.result: QA013.2 uses unique gene segments (VH3-7*01 VD1-1*01 VJ5*02 and VL1-40*01 VJ2*01), has moderate SHM (≤20%), and was not polyreactive.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 characterize basic properties of QA013.2. The gene usage and SHM levels are documented in the lineage analysis (C12-C13, C15-C16). Polyreactivity testing is shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1. These properties distinguish QA013.2 from many other HIV bnAbs.
